questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Conduction velocity of a motor nerve and the delay at the neuromuscular junction from two latencies
questions.question: In a nerve–muscle preparation, the motor nerve is stimulated at point P, 120 mm from the muscle, and the muscle starts to contract 5.0 ms later. When the nerve is stimulated at point Q, 30 mm from the muscle, the delay is 3.2 ms. What is the conduction velocity of the nerve, and how much of the delay is not due to conduction along the nerve (transmission at the junction and the start of contraction)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 50 m s⁻¹; 2.6 ms.
Concept: A nerve impulse travels along an axon as a wave of depolarisation at a fixed speed. At the neuromuscular junction (a chemical synapse) the impulse is passed on by release and diffusion of acetylcholine, which takes extra time (synaptic delay). The total delay = conduction time + a fixed junction and muscle delay.
Given: distances 120 mm and 30 mm; delays 5.0 ms and 3.2 ms.
Formula/Principle: the fixed delay is the same for both points, so the difference in delays is the conduction time over the difference in distance; v = Δd/Δt.
Step 1: v = (120 − 30) mm ÷ (5.0 − 3.2) ms = 90 mm ÷ 1.8 ms = 50 mm ms⁻¹ = 50 m s⁻¹.
Step 2: Conduction time from Q = 30 mm ÷ 50 mm ms⁻¹ = 0.6 ms; fixed delay = 3.2 − 0.6 = 2.6 ms.
Why: Check with P: 120/50 = 2.4 ms + 2.6 ms = 5.0 ms. Using two points cancels the unknown fixed delay, which comes mainly from chemical transmission at the junction.
Why not the others: (A) It takes the whole delay from Q as the fixed delay, ignoring 0.6 ms of conduction. (C) 120 mm ÷ 5.0 ms treats all the delay as conduction. (D) The conduction velocity is wrong by a factor of two, so the fixed delay is also wrong.
Key point: Use two stimulation points: Δdistance ÷ Δlatency = conduction velocity; the rest is synaptic and muscle delay.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Haplodiploid sex determination in honey bees and how drones form sperm
questions.question: In honey bees, a fertilised egg develops into a female (queen or worker) and an unfertilised egg develops into a male (drone). Females have 32 chromosomes. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Drones have 32 chromosomes and form sperm by meiosis
B) A drone has a father and a grandmother but no mother
C) Drones are haploid with 16 chromosomes, form sperm by mitosis, and have a mother and grandparents but no father
D) Sex in honey bees is decided by X and Y chromosomes, as in humans
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Drones are haploid with 16 chromosomes, form sperm by mitosis, and have a mother and grandparents but no father.
Concept: Honey bees show haplodiploid sex determination: the number of chromosome sets decides sex. Diploid individuals (2n = 32) are female; haploid individuals (n = 16), which develop by parthenogenesis from unfertilised eggs, are male.
Why: A drone develops from an unfertilised egg of the queen, so it has a mother but no father, while its mother had both parents, so it has grandparents. Being haploid, it cannot halve its chromosome number again, so it forms sperm by mitosis, and all its sperm are genetically identical.
Why not the others: (A) Drones are haploid (16 chromosomes); meiosis would halve this again. (B) The relationship is reversed: a drone has a mother, not a father. (D) Honey bees have no sex chromosomes; sex depends on ploidy.
Key point: Honey bee: fertilised egg → female (2n = 32); unfertilised egg → male (n = 16), sperm by mitosis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Deducing the mode of inheritance and genotypes from a three-generation pedigree
questions.question: The pedigree shows a rare trait in a family (filled symbols = affected). Assume that II-4 comes from a family with no history of the trait and is homozygous normal. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) The trait is autosomal recessive; I-1 and I-2 are both heterozygous, and III-1 and III-2 are both carriers
B) The trait is X-linked recessive; I-2 is a carrier, and III-1 will be affected
C) The trait is autosomal dominant; I-1 is heterozygous
D) The trait is autosomal recessive; I-1 is homozygous normal and only I-2 is a carrier
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The trait is autosomal recessive; I-1 and I-2 are both heterozygous, and III-1 and III-2 are both carriers.
Concept: Pedigree analysis traces a trait through generations. If two unaffected parents have an affected child, the trait is recessive. If an affected daughter has an unaffected father, the trait cannot be X-linked recessive, because her father would have to carry, and therefore show, the recessive allele on his single X chromosome.
Why: I-1 and I-2 are unaffected but have affected children (II-1 and II-3), so the trait is recessive, and both parents must be heterozygous (Aa). II-1 is an affected daughter of an unaffected father, so the gene is autosomal. II-1 (aa) × II-4 (AA) can only give Aa children, so III-1 and III-2 are unaffected carriers.
Why not the others: (B) For X-linked recessive inheritance, the affected daughter II-1 would need an affected father. Also, III-1 gets his X from II-1 but is unaffected. (C) A dominant trait would appear in at least one parent of each affected child. (D) An aa child needs one a allele from each parent, so I-1 must also be a carrier.
Key point: Unaffected parents with an affected daughter → autosomal recessive; both parents Aa.
questions.image_alt: Three-generation pedigree. Generation I: an unaffected man (I-1) and an unaffected woman (I-2). Generation II: their children are an affected daughter (II-1), an unaffected son (II-2) and an affected son (II-3); II-1 is married to an unaffected man (II-4). Generation III: II-1 and II-4 have an unaffected son (III-1) and an unaffected daughter (III-2).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting the product of a repeating synthetic mRNA in a cell-free translation system
questions.question: A synthetic RNA with the repeating sequence ACACACAC… is added to a cell-free system that contains ribosomes, tRNAs, amino acids and enzymes. The polypeptide made contains threonine and histidine in strict alternation (Thr–His–Thr–His…). The codon ACA codes for threonine and CAC codes for histidine. Which conclusion does this result support?
options: A) The code is a doublet: AC codes for one amino acid
B) Each base is read in two overlapping codons
C) The RNA is translated from both ends at once
D) The code is a triplet read without overlaps in a single frame, so the message is read as ACA, CAC, ACA, CAC…
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The code is a triplet read without overlaps in a single frame, so the message is read as ACA, CAC, ACA, CAC…
Concept: The genetic code is a triplet, non-overlapping and comma-less: the message is read three bases at a time from a fixed starting point. Synthetic RNAs in cell-free systems (Nirenberg, Khorana) were used to decipher the code.
Why: Read in triplets, ACACAC… gives ACA, CAC, ACA, CAC…, i.e. alternating Thr and His, exactly as observed. Wherever reading starts, the triplets alternate between two codons.
Why not the others: (A) A doublet code would read AC, AC, AC…, giving a chain of one amino acid only. (B) Overlapping reading is not supported; most mutations change only one amino acid, and overlapping codons would link neighbouring amino acids rigidly. (C) Ribosomes read mRNA in one direction, 5′ → 3′.
Key point: Repeating dinucleotide RNA → alternating two amino acids → triplet, non-overlapping code.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Coordinate induction of the three lac operon enzymes as evidence of a polycistronic transcript
questions.question:
Lactose is added at time 0 to E. coli growing without glucose or lactose. The amounts (arbitrary units per cell) of three enzymes coded by the lac operon are measured.

Time / min | β-galactosidase (z) | Permease (y) | Transacetylase (a)
0 | 1.0 | 0.5 | 0.2
5 | 40 | 20 | 8
10 | 100 | 50 | 20

Which interpretation best explains the data?
options: A) Each gene has its own operator, and each responds separately to lactose
B) β-galactosidase is made first and then switches on the other two genes
C) The three genes are transcribed together as one polycistronic mRNA from a single promoter under one operator, so they are induced together in a fixed ratio
D) Lactose acts as a corepressor that represses all three genes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The three genes are transcribed together as one polycistronic mRNA from a single promoter under one operator, so they are induced together in a fixed ratio.
Concept: The lac operon has a regulatory gene (i, for the repressor), a promoter, an operator and three structural genes, z, y and a. Without inducer, the repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription. Lactose (as allolactose) inactivates the repressor, and RNA polymerase transcribes all three genes as one mRNA.
Why: The ratio z : y : a stays 10 : 5 : 2 at every time (1.0 : 0.5 : 0.2, 40 : 20 : 8, 100 : 50 : 20). The genes rise together and in step, which shows they are controlled as one unit. The low level at time 0 is the small basal expression, which lets a little lactose enter and be converted to inducer.
Why not the others: (A) Separate control would not keep the ratios exactly constant. (B) All three increase together from the start; y and a do not lag behind z. (D) Lactose is an inducer: enzyme levels rise, not fall, after it is added.
Key point: Operon → one promoter and operator → one polycistronic mRNA → coordinate expression of z, y and a.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Effect of gene flow on allele frequencies of two populations that had diverged by drift
questions.question: Two small, isolated populations of a rodent started with the same allele frequencies. After many generations, the frequency of allele A was 0.2 in one and 0.8 in the other, although their environments were similar. A corridor was then built so that animals could move between them, and after several generations the frequency of A was close to 0.5 in both. Which explanation is best?
options: A) Gene flow (migration) carried alleles between the populations and made their allele frequencies similar, undoing the divergence that genetic drift had caused
B) New mutations to allele A arose in one population and not in the other
C) Natural selection favoured the same allele in both populations after the corridor was built
D) A founder effect occurred when the corridor was built
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Gene flow (migration) carried alleles between the populations and made their allele frequencies similar, undoing the divergence that genetic drift had caused.
Concept: Factors that change allele frequencies (Hardy–Weinberg disturbing factors) include gene flow, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection. Drift, which is random change, is strong in small populations and makes isolated populations diverge. Gene flow mixes the gene pools and makes populations more alike.
Why: With similar environments, the original divergence is best explained by chance (drift) in small populations. Once migration begins, alleles move both ways, and the allele frequencies of the two populations converge towards a common value.
Why not the others: (B) Mutation is too slow to change allele frequencies by this much in a few generations. (C) Selection for the same allele would push both towards 1 or 0, not towards 0.5. (D) A founder effect needs a few individuals starting a new population; it would increase differences, not remove them.
Key point: Drift makes isolated populations diverge; gene flow makes them converge.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Chronological order of forms in human evolution
questions.question: Which sequence lists these forms in the order in which they appeared during human evolution, from earliest to latest?
options: A) Australopithecus → Dryopithecus → Homo habilis → Homo erectus → Homo sapiens
B) Dryopithecus → Homo habilis → Australopithecus → Homo erectus → Homo sapiens
C) Dryopithecus → Australopithecus → Homo erectus → Homo habilis → Homo sapiens
D) Dryopithecus → Australopithecus → Homo habilis → Homo erectus → Homo sapiens
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Dryopithecus → Australopithecus → Homo habilis → Homo erectus → Homo sapiens.
Concept: Fossil evidence shows a gradual change from ape-like primates to modern humans, with increase in brain size, upright posture and use of tools.
Why: About 15 million years ago, Dryopithecus (ape-like) and Ramapithecus (more man-like) lived. About 2 million years ago, australopithecines lived in the East African grasslands; they hunted with stone weapons and mainly ate fruit. Homo habilis, probably the first human-like being, had a brain capacity of 650–800 cc. Homo erectus (about 1.5 million years ago) had about 900 cc. Homo sapiens arose in Africa and spread across continents.
Why not the others: (A) Dryopithecus is much older than Australopithecus. (B) Australopithecines came before the first members of the genus Homo. (C) Homo habilis came before Homo erectus.
Key point: Dryopithecus → Australopithecus → H. habilis → H. erectus → (Neanderthals) → H. sapiens.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Mechanism of an allergic reaction: sensitisation, IgE and mast cells
questions.question: A person sneezes and has watery eyes every time they are exposed to pollen of a certain plant, but not on the very first exposure. Which explanation of this allergy is correct?
options: A) Pollen is a pathogen that multiplies in the nose, and IgG destroys it, causing the symptoms on the first exposure

B) On first exposure, the allergen induces IgE antibodies, which attach to mast cells (sensitisation); on later exposure, the allergen binds this IgE, and mast cells release histamine and serotonin, causing the symptoms, which antihistamines can relieve
C) T cells attack the person's own nasal cells, as in autoimmune disease
D) Plasma cells release histamine directly when pollen touches them
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) On first exposure, the allergen induces IgE antibodies, which attach to mast cells (sensitisation); on later exposure, the allergen binds this IgE, and mast cells release histamine and serotonin, causing the symptoms, which antihistamines can relieve.
Concept: Allergy is an exaggerated immune response to certain harmless antigens (allergens) such as pollen, mites or dust. The antibodies produced are of the IgE type. Chemicals such as histamine and serotonin from mast cells cause the symptoms.
Why: The first exposure only sensitises the person by making IgE that coats mast cells. On re-exposure, the allergen cross-links the bound IgE, and the mast cells release their chemicals, which dilate blood vessels and increase secretions: sneezing, watery eyes and running nose. Antihistamines, adrenaline and steroids reduce the symptoms.
Why not the others: (A) Pollen does not multiply in the body, and the antibody class involved is IgE, not IgG; there are no symptoms on first exposure. (C) Allergy is a response to an outside allergen, not an attack on self cells. (D) Histamine comes from mast cells, not from plasma cells, which secrete antibodies.
Key point: Allergy: first exposure → IgE on mast cells; re-exposure → histamine release.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing DNA isolation from plant cells and bacterial cells
questions.question: DNA is to be isolated from a plant leaf and from a bacterium. Which comparison of the procedures is correct?
options: A) Lysozyme is used to break the cell walls in both cases
B) In both cases the DNA is precipitated by heating the extract to 90 °C
C) Chitinase is used for the plant cells and cellulase for the bacterial cells

D) The wall is broken with cellulase for the plant and lysozyme for the bacterium; in both, RNA and proteins are removed with ribonuclease and protease, and the DNA is precipitated by adding chilled ethanol
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The wall is broken with cellulase for the plant and lysozyme for the bacterium; in both, RNA and proteins are removed with ribonuclease and protease, and the DNA is precipitated by adding chilled ethanol.
Concept: To obtain pure DNA, the cell is opened to release DNA along with RNA, proteins, polysaccharides and lipids. The enzyme for breaking the cell wall depends on what the wall is made of: lysozyme for bacteria, cellulase for plant cells and chitinase for fungi.
Why: Plant walls are mainly cellulose and bacterial walls are peptidoglycan, so different enzymes are needed. After this step the procedures are the same: ribonuclease removes RNA, protease removes proteins (including those bound to DNA), and chilled ethanol precipitates the purified DNA as fine threads that can be spooled out.
Why not the others: (A) Lysozyme does not digest the cellulose of plant walls. (B) DNA is precipitated with chilled ethanol, not by heating. (C) The enzymes are wrong: chitinase is for fungal walls, and cellulase does not digest bacterial walls.
Key point: Wall enzyme varies (lysozyme, cellulase, chitinase); then RNase, protease and chilled ethanol.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Why a recombinant hepatitis B vaccine made in yeast is safe yet protective
questions.question: The gene for the surface antigen protein of hepatitis B virus is inserted into yeast. The yeast cells make this protein, which is purified and injected as a vaccine. Vaccinated people make antibodies against the virus, but nobody catches hepatitis B from the vaccine. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) The yeast makes complete but weakened viruses, which cause a mild infection
B) The vaccine contains only one viral protein and no viral genome, so it cannot replicate, but it still stimulates B and T cells to produce antibodies and memory cells
C) The vaccine supplies ready-made antibodies, giving passive immunity
D) The yeast cells colonise the body and keep making the protein for life
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The vaccine contains only one viral protein and no viral genome, so it cannot replicate, but it still stimulates B and T cells to produce antibodies and memory cells.
Concept: Recombinant DNA technology allows antigenic polypeptides of a pathogen to be produced in bacteria or yeast. These can be used as vaccines (for example, the hepatitis B vaccine produced from yeast). Vaccination gives active immunity.
Why: An infection needs the viral genome to make new viruses. The surface protein alone cannot do this, so it is safe. Still, it carries the antigenic determinants of the virus, so the immune system responds to it, and memory cells then give a quick secondary response if the real virus enters.
Why not the others: (A) Only one protein is made; no virus particles form. (C) Antibodies are made by the vaccinated person, which is active immunity. (D) The yeast cells are used only in the factory; the injected vaccine is purified protein.
Key point: Recombinant subunit vaccine: antigen without genome → active immunity without risk of infection.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Effect of a predator that removes a fixed fraction of prey each year on prey numbers
questions.question: Without predators, a snail population in a pond doubles each year. A predatory fish is introduced that eats 40 % of the snails each year (after breeding). Starting from 1000 snails, how many snails will there be after 3 years with the predator, and how many there would have been without it?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1728; 8000.
Concept: Predation is an interaction in which one species (+) benefits and the other (−) is harmed. Predators keep prey populations in check; without them prey numbers can rise very fast, as when introduced prickly pear spread in Australia until a moth that feeds on it was brought in.
Given: growth factor without predator = 2 per year; 40 % removed each year; N₀ = 1000; t = 3 years.
Formula/Principle: net factor per year = 2 × (1 − 0.40); N = N₀ × (factor)ᵗ.
Step 1: Net factor = 2 × 0.6 = 1.2 per year.
Step 2: With predator: 1000 × 1.2³ = 1000 × 1.728 = 1728; without: 1000 × 2³ = 8000.
Why: The predator does not stop growth here, but it slows it greatly: after 3 years there are fewer than a quarter as many snails as without predation.
Why not the others: (B) The population is not held constant; the net factor 1.2 is still above 1. (C) It subtracts 40 % of the starting number each year (linear), not 40 % of the current number. (D) 6000 assumes the population grows by 2000 each year instead of doubling.
Key point: Fractional removal multiplies the growth factor: 2 × 0.6 = 1.2 per year.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Why organic matter accumulates as peat in a cold waterlogged bog
questions.question: In a cold, waterlogged, acidic bog, dead plant material builds up over thousands of years as peat, whereas in a warm, moist, well-aerated forest soil, leaf litter disappears within a year or two. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) No detritus falls into bogs, so no decomposition is needed
B) Bogs contain more decomposers than forest soil, which turn litter into peat

C) Waterlogging keeps oxygen low, and together with low temperature and acidity this slows the activity of decomposers, so fragmentation, catabolism and mineralisation are slow and organic matter accumulates
D) Bog plants contain no lignin or cellulose, so they cannot be decomposed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Waterlogging keeps oxygen low, and together with low temperature and acidity this slows the activity of decomposers, so fragmentation, catabolism and mineralisation are slow and organic matter accumulates.
Concept: Decomposition includes fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification and mineralisation. Its rate depends on the chemical composition of detritus and on climate. It is fast when the detritus is rich in nitrogen and sugars and the conditions are warm, moist and aerobic. It is slow when the detritus is rich in lignin and chitin, and in cold or anaerobic conditions.
Why: Bacteria and fungi need oxygen for most decomposition, and their enzymes work slowly at low temperature and low pH. In the bog all these factors act together, so plant remains are only partly broken down and build up as peat.
Why not the others: (A) Bog plants die and fall into the bog all the time; the detritus is plentiful. (B) Decomposer activity is lower in bogs, not higher. (D) Bog plants such as mosses do contain cellulose and related compounds; the problem is slow decomposition, not absence of these compounds.
Key point: Decomposition slows down in cold, anaerobic and acidic conditions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Estimating the present extinction rate from the background rate and a multiplying factor
questions.question: Assume that the world has about 7 million species and that the background (natural) extinction rate is about 1 species per million species per year. If the present extinction rate is 1000 times the background rate, about how many species are being lost per year, and about how many per day?
options: A) About 7000 per year; about 19 per day
B) About 7 per year; about 0.02 per day
C) About 70 000 per year; about 192 per day
D) About 7000 per year; about 7 per day
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) About 7000 per year; about 19 per day.
Concept: Species have always gone extinct at a slow background rate. Human activities — habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasions and co-extinctions (the "evil quartet") — are now causing extinctions 100 to 1000 times faster than this.
Given: 7 × 10⁶ species; background rate = 1 per 10⁶ species per year; present rate = 1000 × background.
Formula/Principle: extinctions per year = number of species × rate per species per year.
Step 1: Background: 7 × 10⁶ × 10⁻⁶ = 7 species per year.
Step 2: Present: 7 × 1000 = 7000 per year; per day = 7000 ÷ 365 ≈ 19.
Why: Even a small rate per species becomes large when multiplied by millions of species and by a factor of 1000.
Why not the others: (B) This is the background rate, not the present rate. (C) It uses a factor of 10 000. (D) It divides by 1000 instead of 365 to get the daily figure.
Key point: Present extinction rates are about 100–1000 times the background rate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Matching common fungi with the class and feature that identifies them
questions.question:
Match each fungus with the class to which it belongs and its feature.
Fungi: P Albugo (white rust of mustard); Q Neurospora; R Ustilago (smut); S Alternaria.
Features: (1) Phycomycetes: aseptate, coenocytic mycelium; asexual spores are zoospores or aplanospores; (2) Ascomycetes: sexual spores (ascospores) formed inside sac-like asci; (3) Basidiomycetes: sexual spores (basidiospores) on basidia; no sex organs, plasmogamy by fusion of somatic cells; (4) Deuteromycetes: only asexual (conidial) stages known.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) P-1, Q-2, R-3, S-4.
Concept: Fungi are classified mainly by the morphology of the mycelium, the mode of spore formation and the fruiting bodies.
Why: Albugo, a parasite on mustard, is a phycomycete with aseptate coenocytic hyphae (P-1). Neurospora, used widely in genetics, is an ascomycete forming ascospores in asci (Q-2). Ustilago, which causes smut, is a basidiomycete (R-3). Alternaria is a deuteromycete (a "fungus imperfecti") in which only asexual conidia are known (S-4).
Why not the others: (A) Albugo has aseptate hyphae (Phycomycetes), and Neurospora is an ascomycete. (B) Neurospora and Ustilago are swapped. (C) Albugo and Alternaria are swapped.
Key point: Albugo – Phycomycetes; Neurospora – Ascomycetes; Ustilago – Basidiomycetes; Alternaria – Deuteromycetes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Order of tissues from the outside to the centre of a young dicot stem
questions.question: Arrange these tissues of a transverse section of a young dicot stem (such as sunflower) from the outside towards the centre: P endodermis (starch sheath); Q hypodermis of collenchyma; R pith; S pericycle with patches of sclerenchyma; T vascular bundles arranged in a ring.
options: A) P → Q → S → T → R
B) Q → P → S → T → R
C) Q → S → P → T → R
D) Q → P → T → S → R
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Q → P → S → T → R.
Concept: A young dicot stem has, from outside inwards: epidermis with cuticle, cortex (hypodermis of collenchyma, then parenchyma, then endodermis), and then the stele (pericycle, vascular bundles in a ring, and pith).
Why: Just below the epidermis is the collenchymatous hypodermis (Q). The innermost layer of the cortex is the endodermis, rich in starch grains (P). Inside it, the pericycle has semilunar patches of sclerenchyma (S). Then come the conjoint, open vascular bundles arranged in a ring (T), and the centre is filled with parenchymatous pith (R).
Why not the others: (A) The endodermis is the innermost layer of the cortex, so the hypodermis lies outside it. (C) The pericycle is part of the stele and lies inside the endodermis. (D) The pericycle lies outside the vascular bundles.
Key point: Dicot stem: hypodermis → cortex → endodermis → pericycle → ring of bundles → pith.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Effects of colchicine and cytochalasin on dividing cells, and which cytoskeletal elements they act on
questions.question: Colchicine added to dividing cells stops them at metaphase, and in plants it can give polyploid cells. Cytochalasin B added to animal cells stops cytoplasmic streaming and the formation of the cleavage furrow, but does not stop the spindle from forming. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) Colchicine disrupts actin microfilaments, and cytochalasin disrupts microtubules
B) Both drugs act on microtubules
C) Colchicine prevents the assembly of tubulin into microtubules, so no spindle forms; cytochalasin disrupts actin microfilaments, which drive streaming and the cleavage furrow
D) Both drugs act on intermediate filaments
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Colchicine prevents the assembly of tubulin into microtubules, so no spindle forms; cytochalasin disrupts actin microfilaments, which drive streaming and the cleavage furrow.
Concept: The cytoskeleton is a network of protein filaments: microtubules (tubulin), microfilaments (actin) and intermediate filaments. Microtubules form the spindle fibres, cilia, flagella and centrioles; microfilaments help in cell movement, cytoplasmic streaming and the contractile ring of animal cytokinesis.
Why: Without a spindle, chromosomes cannot separate, so cells stay in metaphase, and if the cell recovers without dividing, its chromosome number is doubled (polyploidy). Cytochalasin targets actin, so streaming and the actin ring of the cleavage furrow fail, while the tubulin spindle is unaffected.
Why not the others: (A) The targets are swapped; the spindle is made of microtubules. (B) Cytochalasin leaves the spindle intact, so it does not act on microtubules. (D) Intermediate filaments are not responsible for the spindle or for streaming.
Key point: Spindle = microtubules (blocked by colchicine); streaming and cleavage furrow = actin (blocked by cytochalasin).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reaction rate at a given substrate concentration and the concentration needed for 90 % of Vmax
questions.question: An enzyme follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics with \(K_m=2.0\) mmol L⁻¹ and \(V_{\max}=100\) units. What is the rate when [S] = 6.0 mmol L⁻¹, and what substrate concentration is needed for the rate to reach 90 units?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 75 units; 18 mmol L⁻¹.
Concept: For many enzymes the rate rises with substrate concentration and levels off at Vmax, when all active sites are occupied. \(K_m\) is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of Vmax; it measures the affinity of the enzyme for its substrate.
Given: \(K_m=2.0\) mmol L⁻¹; \(V_{\max}=100\); [S] = 6.0 mmol L⁻¹; target v = 90.
Formula/Principle: \(v=\dfrac{V_{\max}[S]}{K_m+[S]}\).
Step 1: \(v=\dfrac{100\times6.0}{2.0+6.0}=75\) units.
Step 2: \(90=\dfrac{100[S]}{2.0+[S]}\Rightarrow 180+90[S]=100[S]\Rightarrow[S]=18\) mmol L⁻¹.
Why: To reach 90 % of Vmax, [S] must be 9 times Km. Increasing [S] gives smaller and smaller increases in rate because the enzyme approaches saturation.
Why not the others: (A) 50 units is the rate at [S] = Km, not at 3 Km. (C) 12 mmol L⁻¹ gives 100 × 12/14 ≈ 86 units. (D) The rate can never exceed Vmax.
Key point: \(v=V_{\max}[S]/(K_m+[S])\); [S] = Km → ½ Vmax; [S] = 9 Km → 0.9 Vmax.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing prophase I of meiosis with prophase of mitosis
questions.question: Which statement correctly compares prophase I of meiosis with prophase of mitosis?
options: A) In prophase I, crossing over occurs during zygotene between sister chromatids of the same chromosome
B) The chromosome number is halved during prophase I
C) A synaptonemal complex forms between homologous chromosomes in mitotic prophase as well

D) In prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis in zygotene), exchange segments (crossing over in pachytene) and show chiasmata (diplotene); none of these happens in mitotic prophase, where homologues behave independently
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) In prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis in zygotene), exchange segments (crossing over in pachytene) and show chiasmata (diplotene); none of these happens in mitotic prophase, where homologues behave independently.
Concept: Prophase I is long and has five substages: leptotene (chromosomes become visible), zygotene (synapsis, synaptonemal complex forms), pachytene (crossing over between non-sister chromatids, using recombinase), diplotene (synaptonemal complex dissolves, chiasmata visible) and diakinesis (terminalisation of chiasmata).
Why: Pairing and crossing over are special to meiosis and give genetic recombination. In mitosis each chromosome condenses and acts on its own, so daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent.
Why not the others: (A) Crossing over occurs in pachytene and between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes. (B) The number is halved only when homologues separate at anaphase I and the cell divides. (C) The synaptonemal complex forms only in meiosis.
Key point: Synapsis (zygotene), crossing over (pachytene), chiasmata (diplotene) — unique to prophase I.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Sequence of reactions and organelles in photorespiration
questions.question:
The following events take place during photorespiration in a C₃ plant.
P: Glycolate enters the peroxisome and is converted to glycine.
Q: RuBisCO combines RuBP with O₂, giving one 3-PGA and one phosphoglycolate.
R: Glycine enters the mitochondrion; two glycines give one serine, and CO₂ is released.
S: Phosphoglycolate is converted to glycolate in the chloroplast.
T: Serine is converted via the peroxisome to glycerate, which returns to the chloroplast and the Calvin cycle.
Which order is correct?
options: A) Q → P → S → R → T
B) S → Q → P → R → T
C) Q → S → P → R → T
D) Q → S → R → P → T
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Q → S → P → R → T.
Concept: RuBisCO can bind both CO₂ and O₂. When it binds O₂ (oxygenation), the pathway called photorespiration follows, involving chloroplasts, peroxisomes and mitochondria. It releases CO₂ that had already been fixed, and makes neither sugar nor ATP. C₄ plants avoid it by raising the CO₂ level around RuBisCO in bundle-sheath cells.
Why: Oxygenation of RuBP starts the pathway (Q). Phosphoglycolate is dephosphorylated to glycolate in the chloroplast (S). Glycolate is converted to glycine in the peroxisome (P). In the mitochondrion, two glycines give serine and CO₂ (R) — the step where carbon is lost. Serine returns through the peroxisome as glycerate to the chloroplast (T).
Why not the others: (A) Phosphoglycolate must become glycolate before it leaves the chloroplast for the peroxisome. (B) Phosphoglycolate is a product of the oxygenation step, so it cannot come first. (D) Glycine is made in the peroxisome before it reaches the mitochondrion.
Key point: Photorespiration: chloroplast → peroxisome → mitochondrion (CO₂ lost) → back to chloroplast.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: ATP formed and oxygen used when one pyruvate is completely oxidised in the mitochondrion
questions.question: One molecule of pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is completely oxidised through the link reaction and the Krebs cycle, with the reduced coenzymes passing through the electron transport system. Taking 3 ATP per NADH and 2 ATP per FADH₂, how many ATP are formed in all, and how many molecules of O₂ are used?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 15 ATP; 2.5 O₂.
Concept: The link reaction (pyruvate → acetyl CoA) gives one NADH. The Krebs cycle gives 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 GTP (ATP) per acetyl CoA. In the electron transport system, electrons from NADH and FADH₂ are passed to O₂, the final acceptor, and the energy is used for ATP synthesis (oxidative phosphorylation).
Given: per pyruvate: 4 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP; 3 ATP per NADH, 2 ATP per FADH₂.
Formula/Principle: ATP = 3 × NADH + 2 × FADH₂ + substrate-level ATP; each NADH or FADH₂ gives 2 electrons, and ½ O₂ accepts 2 electrons.
Step 1: ATP = 3 × 4 + 2 × 1 + 1 = 15.
Step 2: Electron pairs = 4 + 1 = 5; O₂ = 5 × ½ = 2.5 molecules.
Why: Two pyruvates come from one glucose, so this gives 30 ATP and 5 O₂ from pyruvate; adding glycolysis gives the textbook 38 ATP and 6 O₂ per glucose.
Why not the others: (B) It counts only one acetyl CoA in the Krebs cycle and leaves out the NADH of the link reaction. (C) It takes one O₂ per electron pair instead of ½ O₂. (D) These are the values for a whole glucose molecule.
Key point: Per pyruvate: 4 NADH + 1 FADH₂ + 1 GTP → 15 ATP, using 2.5 O₂.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Linked: dipeptides from glycine and alanine, their molar mass, and the level of protein structure kept on denaturation
questions.question: Glycine (molar mass 75 g mol⁻¹) and alanine (89 g mol⁻¹) are joined by one peptide bond. How many different dipeptides containing one glycine and one alanine residue are possible, and what is their molar mass? When egg albumin is denatured by boiling, which level of protein structure remains intact?
options: A) 1 dipeptide; 164 g mol⁻¹; primary structure
B) 2 dipeptides; 164 g mol⁻¹; secondary structure
C) 2 dipeptides; 146 g mol⁻¹; primary structure
D) 4 dipeptides; 146 g mol⁻¹; tertiary structure
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2 dipeptides; 146 g mol⁻¹; primary structure.
Concept: A peptide bond (–CO–NH–) forms between the –COOH of one amino acid and the –NH₂ of another, with loss of one water molecule. A peptide has an N-terminal end and a C-terminal end, so Gly–Ala and Ala–Gly are different compounds. Denaturation disrupts hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions, so the secondary and tertiary structures are lost, but the covalent peptide bonds (primary structure) remain.
Why: Gly–Ala (glycylalanine) and Ala–Gly (alanylglycine) are the two possibilities. Molar mass = 75 + 89 − 18 = 146 g mol⁻¹. Boiling coagulates egg albumin by unfolding the chains, but does not hydrolyse peptide bonds, so the amino-acid sequence is unchanged.
Why not the others: (A) The order of residues matters, so there are two dipeptides; and water is lost, so 164 is wrong. (B) Secondary structure (α-helix, β-sheet) is held by hydrogen bonds, which are broken on denaturation. (D) Gly–Gly and Ala–Ala do not contain one residue of each; tertiary structure is lost on denaturation.
Key point: Peptide bond = condensation (−H₂O); denaturation destroys 2° and 3° structure but keeps the 1° sequence.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Empirical and molecular formula of a hydrocarbon from percentage composition and vapour volume, and its possible structures
questions.question: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7 % carbon and 14.3 % hydrogen by mass. At STP, 0.21 g of its vapour occupies 112 mL. What are its empirical and molecular formulae, and how many structures (constitutional isomers) are possible for it? (C = 12, H = 1; molar volume at STP = 22.4 L)
options: A) CH₂; C₃H₆; two (propene and cyclopropane)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) CH₂; C₃H₆; two (propene and cyclopropane).
Concept: The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of it, fixed by the molar mass. A formula CₙH₂ₙ corresponds to one degree of unsaturation: either one C=C bond or one ring.
Given: C 85.7 %, H 14.3 %; 0.21 g occupies 112 mL at STP.
Formula/Principle: mole ratio = (% ÷ atomic mass); M = mass ÷ moles; n = M ÷ (empirical formula mass).
Step 1: C: 85.7/12 = 7.14; H: 14.3/1 = 14.3; ratio 1 : 2 → CH₂ (formula mass 14).
Step 2: Moles = 0.112/22.4 = 0.0050; M = 0.21/0.0050 = 42 g mol⁻¹; n = 42/14 = 3 → C₃H₆.
Why: C₃H₆ can be CH₂=CH–CH₃ (propene) or a three-membered ring (cyclopropane), two constitutional isomers.
Why not the others: (B) C₂H₄ would have M = 28. (C) The H : C ratio is 2, not 3. (D) It misses the ring isomer, cyclopropane.
Key point: Empirical formula from % composition; molecular formula from molar mass; CₙH₂ₙ = alkene or cycloalkane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: De Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 150 V and of a cricket ball
questions.question: In an electron diffraction experiment, electrons starting from rest are accelerated through a potential difference of 150 V. What is their de Broglie wavelength, and what is the de Broglie wavelength of a 0.15 kg cricket ball moving at 30 m s⁻¹? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg; e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0.10 nm; about \(1.5\times10^{-34}\) m.
Concept: De Broglie proposed that every moving particle has a wavelength \(\lambda=h/p=h/mv\). For an electron accelerated through V volts, \(eV=p^2/2m\), so \(\lambda=h/\sqrt{2meV}\).
Given: V = 150 V; mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg; ball: m = 0.15 kg, v = 30 m s⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: \(\lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}\) (electron); \(\lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv}\) (ball).
Step 1: \(p=\sqrt{2\times9.11\times10^{-31}\times1.60\times10^{-19}\times150}=6.61\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\); \(\lambda=6.63\times10^{-34}/6.61\times10^{-24}=1.0\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm m=0.10\) nm.
Step 2: Ball: \(\lambda=6.63\times10^{-34}/(0.15\times30)=1.5\times10^{-34}\) m.
Why: 0.10 nm is about the spacing of atoms in a crystal, so a crystal acts as a diffraction grating for such electrons (as in the Davisson–Germer experiment). The ball's wavelength is far smaller than any object, so its wave nature cannot be observed.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) are wrong by a factor of 10 for the electron. (C) The ball's momentum is 4.5 kg m s⁻¹, which gives about 10⁻³⁴ m, not 10⁻²⁰ m.
Key point: λ = h/p; noticeable only for very small masses such as electrons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Linked: highest oxidation state shown by period 3 elements in their oxides, and the acid–base nature of the oxides
questions.question: Consider the highest oxides of the period 3 elements from sodium to chlorine. Which element shows the oxidation state +7 in its oxide, what is the nature of that oxide, and which oxide of the series is amphoteric?
options: A) Sulfur; SO₃ is basic; MgO is amphoteric
B) Chlorine; Cl₂O₇ is basic; Al₂O₃ is amphoteric
C) Phosphorus; P₄O₁₀ is acidic; SiO₂ is amphoteric
D) Chlorine; Cl₂O₇ is strongly acidic; Al₂O₃ is amphoteric
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Chlorine; Cl₂O₇ is strongly acidic; Al₂O₃ is amphoteric.
Concept: For main-group elements the highest oxidation state usually equals the number of valence electrons (for groups 13–17, group number − 10). Across a period, oxides change from basic (metals) through amphoteric to acidic (non-metals).
Why: The highest oxides are Na₂O (+1), MgO (+2), Al₂O₃ (+3), SiO₂ (+4), P₄O₁₀ (+5), SO₃ (+6) and Cl₂O₇ (+7). Na₂O and MgO are basic; Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids and bases (amphoteric); SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃ and Cl₂O₇ are acidic, with Cl₂O₇ (the anhydride of HClO₄) the most strongly acidic.
Why not the others: (A) Sulfur reaches only +6, and SO₃ is acidic; MgO is basic. (B) Cl₂O₇ is acidic, not basic. (C) Phosphorus reaches +5, and SiO₂ is acidic.
Key point: Period 3 highest oxides: basic → amphoteric (Al₂O₃) → acidic; Cl reaches +7 in Cl₂O₇.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Hybridisation involving d orbitals and the resulting molecular shapes
questions.question: Which molecule is correctly matched with the hybridisation of its central atom and its shape?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\ce{BrF5}\): sp³d², square pyramidal.
Concept: The number of electron pairs (bond pairs + lone pairs) on the central atom decides the hybridisation: 4 → sp³, 5 → sp³d, 6 → sp³d². Lone pairs occupy some of the hybrid orbitals, so the shape (positions of the atoms) can differ from the electron-pair geometry.
Why: Br has 7 valence electrons; 5 are used in Br–F bonds, leaving 1 lone pair. Six electron pairs give sp³d² (octahedral arrangement); with one position taken by a lone pair, the shape is square pyramidal.
Why not the others: (B) XeF₄ has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs: sp³d², square planar. (C) ClF₃ has 3 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs: sp³d, T-shaped (the lone pairs occupy equatorial positions). (D) SF₆ has 6 bond pairs: sp³d², octahedral.
Key point: 5 pairs → sp³d; 6 pairs → sp³d²; lone pairs change the shape, not the hybridisation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ordering reactions by the temperature above which they become spontaneous
questions.question:
Three reactions have the following values, which may be taken as independent of temperature.

Reaction | ΔH / kJ mol⁻¹ | ΔS / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
R1 | +50 | +100
R2 | +40 | +200
R3 | +90 | +150

Which is the correct increasing order of the temperature above which each reaction becomes spontaneous?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) R2 < R1 < R3.
Concept: \(\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S\). When both ΔH and ΔS are positive, the reaction is non-spontaneous at low temperature and spontaneous above \(T=\Delta H/\Delta S\), where ΔG = 0 (equilibrium).
Given: ΔH and ΔS for R1, R2 and R3.
Formula/Principle: \(T_{\min}=\Delta H/\Delta S\) (ΔH in J mol⁻¹).
Step 1: R1: 50 000/100 = 500 K; R2: 40 000/200 = 200 K.
Step 2: R3: 90 000/150 = 600 K.
Why: So R2 (200 K) < R1 (500 K) < R3 (600 K). A reaction becomes spontaneous at a lower temperature when its ΔS is large compared with its ΔH.
Why not the others: (A) It orders by ΔH alone. (B) It orders by ΔS, from smallest to largest, but reverses the effect. (D) R3 needs 600 K, the highest of the three.
Key point: ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0: spontaneous only above \(T=\Delta H/\Delta S\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: pH of acetic acid–acetate mixtures from the Henderson equation, and the mixture with the best buffer capacity
questions.question:
Three mixtures are made from ethanoic acid (pKa = 4.74) and sodium ethanoate.

Mixture | [CH₃COOH] / mol L⁻¹ | [CH₃COO⁻] / mol L⁻¹
(i) | 0.10 | 0.10
(ii) | 0.10 | 0.010
(iii) | 0.010 | 0.10

What is the pH of mixture (iii), and which mixture best resists a change in pH when either a little acid or a little base is added?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 5.74; mixture (i).
Concept: For an acidic buffer, the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is \(\text{pH}=\text{p}K_a+\log\dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}\). A buffer resists change best (largest buffer capacity) when acid and conjugate base are present in equal, fairly large amounts, i.e. when pH = pKa.
Why: For (iii): pH = 4.74 + log(0.10/0.010) = 4.74 + 1 = 5.74. Mixture (i) has equal amounts of a fairly large concentration of acid and base (pH 4.74), so it can neutralise both added H⁺ (using acetate) and added OH⁻ (using acetic acid) best. In (ii) and (iii) one component is scarce, so the buffer is easily used up in one direction.
Why not the others: (A) 3.74 is the pH of (ii); the sign of the log term is reversed. (B) The pH is right, but (iii) has very little acid to neutralise added base. (C) 4.74 is the pH of (i), and (ii) has very little acetate to neutralise added acid.
Key point: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]); best buffering when [A⁻] = [HA].

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Molarity of potassium permanganate from a titration against oxalic acid, and the indicator used
questions.question: 25.0 mL of 0.050 mol L⁻¹ oxalic acid is acidified with dilute sulfuric acid, warmed and titrated with potassium permanganate solution; 20.0 mL is needed. What is the molarity of the permanganate solution, and how is the end point detected?
options: B) 0.025 mol L⁻¹; the first permanent pale pink colour of excess permanganate (self-indicator)
C) 0.0625 mol L⁻¹; the first permanent pale pink colour (self-indicator)
D) 0.025 mol L⁻¹; with methyl orange
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0.025 mol L⁻¹; the first permanent pale pink colour of excess permanganate (self-indicator).
Concept: In acid solution, permanganate is reduced to colourless Mn²⁺ (gaining 5 electrons) and oxalate is oxidised to CO₂ (losing 2 electrons): \(\ce{2MnO4- + 5C2O4^2- + 16H+ -> 2Mn^2+ + 10CO2 + 8H2O}\). Because MnO₄⁻ is intensely purple and Mn²⁺ almost colourless, the first drop in excess colours the solution pink.
Given: 25.0 mL of 0.050 M oxalic acid; 20.0 mL of KMnO₄.
Formula/Principle: n(MnO₄⁻) = (2/5) × n(oxalate); c = n/V.
Step 1: n(oxalate) = 0.0250 L × 0.050 = 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol.
Step 2: n(MnO₄⁻) = 0.4 × 1.25 × 10⁻³ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol; c = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴/0.0200 = 0.025 mol L⁻¹.
Why: Electrons balance: 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 5 = 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol electrons gained = 1.25 × 10⁻³ × 2 lost. No added indicator is needed.
Why not the others: (A) It inverts the 2 : 5 ratio, and an acid–base indicator does not show a redox end point. (C) It assumes a 1 : 1 ratio. (D) The concentration is right, but methyl orange is not used; permanganate is its own indicator.
Key point: MnO₄⁻ (5e⁻) : C₂O₄²⁻ (2e⁻) = 2 : 5; KMnO₄ acts as a self-indicator.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: Relative rates of precipitation of AgBr from three alkyl bromides, explained by carbocation stability
questions.question: Three alkyl bromides are added separately to a solution of silver nitrate in ethanol at room temperature. 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane gives a cream precipitate at once, 2-bromopropane gives one after a few minutes, and 1-bromopropane gives one only on warming. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) The reaction is SN2, and the order reflects decreasing steric hindrance from tertiary to primary
B) The primary bromide reacts fastest because its C–Br bond is the weakest

C) Ag⁺ helps the C–Br bond ionise, and the rate follows the stability of the carbocation formed: tertiary > secondary > primary, because more alkyl groups stabilise the positive charge by inductive effect and hyperconjugation
D) The C–Br bond becomes stronger from tertiary to primary because of increasing electronegativity of carbon
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Ag⁺ helps the C–Br bond ionise, and the rate follows the stability of the carbocation formed: tertiary > secondary > primary, because more alkyl groups stabilise the positive charge by inductive effect and hyperconjugation.
Concept: Carbocations are stabilised by electron-releasing alkyl groups (+I effect) and by hyperconjugation with adjacent C–H bonds. Stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl. In SN1-type reactions, the slow step is formation of the carbocation, so a more stable carbocation forms faster.
Why: Ag⁺ pulls bromide away as insoluble AgBr. The tertiary bromide gives the stable (CH₃)₃C⁺ (9 hyperconjugating C–H bonds), so the precipitate appears at once; the secondary cation (6 C–H) forms more slowly; the primary cation is so unstable that reaction needs heating.
Why not the others: (A) Steric hindrance would make SN2 fastest for the primary bromide, the opposite of what is seen. (B) The primary bromide reacts slowest. (D) The differences arise from carbocation stability, not from large differences in C–Br bond strength or carbon electronegativity.
Key point: SN1 rate: 3° > 2° > 1°, following carbocation stability.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Percentage yield in the nitration of benzene and the electrophile involved
questions.question: 7.8 g of benzene is heated with a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids, and 9.84 g of nitrobenzene is obtained. What is the percentage yield, and what is the electrophile that attacks the ring? (C = 12, H = 1, N = 14, O = 16)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 80 %; nitronium ion, \(\ce{NO2+}\).
Concept: Nitration is an electrophilic substitution: \(\ce{HNO3 + 2H2SO4 -> NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4-}\). The nitronium ion attacks the π electrons of benzene to form a carbocation (σ-complex), which loses H⁺ to restore the aromatic ring.
Given: 7.8 g benzene (M = 78); 9.84 g nitrobenzene (M = 123); 1 : 1 reaction.
Formula/Principle: theoretical yield = moles of benzene × M(nitrobenzene); % yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100.
Step 1: Benzene = 7.8/78 = 0.10 mol → theoretical nitrobenzene = 0.10 × 123 = 12.3 g.
Step 2: % yield = 9.84/12.3 × 100 = 80 %.
Why: The yield is below 100 % because of incomplete reaction and losses during separation; the sulfuric acid helps to generate the electrophile.
Why not the others: (A) The electrophile must be positive; NO₂⁻ is a nucleophile. (B) It divides the mass of product by the mass of benzene, ignoring molar masses. (C) It makes a decimal error.
Key point: % yield uses moles; nitration electrophile = NO₂⁺.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Molar mass of a non-volatile solute from the relative lowering of vapour pressure
questions.question:
At a certain temperature, the vapour pressure of pure water is 24.00 mm Hg. A solution of 10.0 g of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute in 90.0 g of water has the vapour pressure shown.

Liquid | Vapour pressure / mm Hg
Pure water | 24.00
Solution | 23.76

What is the approximate molar mass of the solute? (H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) About 200 g mol⁻¹.
Concept: By Raoult's law, the relative lowering of vapour pressure of a solvent by a non-volatile solute equals the mole fraction of the solute: \(\dfrac{p^\circ-p}{p^\circ}=x_2=\dfrac{n_2}{n_1+n_2}\approx\dfrac{n_2}{n_1}\) for dilute solutions. It is a colligative property.
Given: \(p^\circ=24.00\), p = 23.76 mm Hg; 10.0 g solute; 90.0 g water.
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{p^\circ-p}{p^\circ}=\dfrac{n_2}{n_1+n_2}\); \(M_2=w_2/n_2\).
Step 1: Relative lowering = 0.24/24.00 = 0.010; \(n_1=90.0/18=5.0\) mol.
Step 2: \(n_2/(5.0+n_2)=0.010\Rightarrow n_2=0.0505\) mol; \(M_2=10.0/0.0505\approx198\approx200\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\).
Why: The dilute-solution approximation (n₂/n₁ = 0.010, n₂ = 0.050 mol) gives exactly 200 g mol⁻¹; the full expression gives 198 g mol⁻¹.
Why not the others: (B) It uses the absolute lowering in a ratio wrongly, a factor of 10 off. (C) It is 10 times too large. (D) It takes the mass of the solution, 100 g, instead of the moles of water.
Key point: Relative lowering of vapour pressure = mole fraction of solute.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Why limiting molar conductivity of a weak base is obtained by Kohlrausch's law, and the correct combination
questions.question: The limiting molar conductivity of \(\ce{NH4OH}\) cannot be obtained reliably by extrapolating a graph of \(\Lambda_m\) against \(\sqrt c\). Which option gives the reason and the correct way to obtain it?
options: A) \(\Lambda_m\) of a weak electrolyte is independent of concentration; \(\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4OH})=\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4Cl})+\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NaCl})-\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NaOH})\)

B) For a weak electrolyte \(\Lambda_m\) rises very steeply at low concentration because the degree of ionisation increases, so the graph cannot be extrapolated; \(\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4OH})=\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4Cl})+\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NaOH})-\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NaCl})\)
C) The graph is a straight line for a weak electrolyte as for a strong one, so extrapolation works well
D) \(\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4OH})=\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4Cl})+\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NaOH})\), because both salts contain the needed ions
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) For a weak electrolyte \(\Lambda_m\) rises very steeply at low concentration because the degree of ionisation increases, so the graph cannot be extrapolated; \(\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4OH})=\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4Cl})+\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NaOH})-\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NaCl})\).
Concept: Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions: at infinite dilution, the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and anion, \(\Lambda^\circ=\nu_+\lambda^\circ_++\nu_-\lambda^\circ_-\).
Why: \(\lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4+})+\lambda^\circ(\ce{Cl-})+\lambda^\circ(\ce{Na+})+\lambda^\circ(\ce{OH-})-\lambda^\circ(\ce{Na+})-\lambda^\circ(\ce{Cl-})=\lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4+})+\lambda^\circ(\ce{OH-})\). All three salts on the right are strong electrolytes, whose \(\Lambda^\circ\) values can be found by extrapolation. For NH₄OH, \(\Lambda_m\) keeps rising sharply as c → 0, so the intercept cannot be read.
Why not the others: (A) \(\Lambda_m\) of a weak electrolyte changes greatly with concentration, and the combination gives \(\lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4+})+2\lambda^\circ(\ce{Cl-})-\lambda^\circ(\ce{OH-})\). (C) The graph is strongly curved for a weak electrolyte. (D) The sum contains extra Na⁺ and Cl⁻ contributions, which must be removed by subtracting \(\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NaCl})\).
Key point: Weak electrolyte: \(\Lambda^\circ\) from Kohlrausch combinations of strong electrolytes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Effect of a catalyst lowering activation energy, and of a 10 K rise, on the rate constant (Arrhenius equation)
questions.question: A reaction has activation energy 50.0 kJ mol⁻¹. (i) A catalyst lowers the activation energy by 20.0 kJ mol⁻¹ without changing the pre-exponential factor; by about what factor does the rate constant increase at 300 K? (ii) Without the catalyst, by about what factor does the rate constant increase when the temperature is raised from 300 K to 310 K? (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) About 3000; about 1.9.
Concept: Arrhenius equation: \(k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}\). A catalyst gives an alternative path with lower activation energy, so many more molecules have enough energy to react. Raising the temperature increases the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Eₐ.
Given: Eₐ = 50.0 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔEₐ = 20.0 kJ mol⁻¹; T = 300 K and 310 K.
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{k_{\text{cat}}}{k}=e^{\Delta E_a/RT}\); \(\ln\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}=\dfrac{E_a}{R}\left(\dfrac1{T_1}-\dfrac1{T_2}\right)\).
Step 1: \(\Delta E_a/RT=20000/(8.314\times300)=8.02\); \(e^{8.02}\approx3.0\times10^{3}\).
Step 2: \(\ln(k_{310}/k_{300})=\dfrac{50000}{8.314}\left(\dfrac1{300}-\dfrac1{310}\right)=6014\times1.075\times10^{-4}=0.647\); \(k_{310}/k_{300}=e^{0.647}\approx1.9\).
Why: The exponential form makes a modest drop in Eₐ very powerful, while a 10 K rise roughly doubles the rate for an activation energy near 50 kJ mol⁻¹ (the familiar rule of thumb).
Why not the others: (A) 8 is the exponent, not the factor \(e^{8}\). (B) 1.03 is the ratio of the temperatures, not of the rate constants. (C) It treats the factor as proportional to ΔEₐ.
Key point: \(k\propto e^{-E_a/RT}\): lowering Eₐ by 20 kJ at 300 K raises k about 3000-fold.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Trend in basicity of lanthanoid hydroxides and its cause
questions.question: Which option gives the correct order of basic strength of the hydroxides La(OH)₃, Gd(OH)₃ and Lu(OH)₃, with the correct reason?
options: A) Lu(OH)₃ > Gd(OH)₃ > La(OH)₃, because lutetium has the largest atomic mass
B) All three are equally basic, because all the ions carry a charge of +3
C) La(OH)₃ > Gd(OH)₃ > Lu(OH)₃, because the Ln³⁺ ions become smaller across the series (lanthanoid contraction, due to poor shielding by 4f electrons), so the Ln–OH bond becomes more covalent
D) La(OH)₃ > Gd(OH)₃ > Lu(OH)₃, because the 4f electrons shield the nucleus very effectively, so the ions become larger
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) La(OH)₃ > Gd(OH)₃ > Lu(OH)₃, because the Ln³⁺ ions become smaller across the series (lanthanoid contraction, due to poor shielding by 4f electrons), so the Ln–OH bond becomes more covalent.
Concept: Lanthanoid contraction is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii from La to Lu. Each added 4f electron shields the added nuclear charge poorly, so the effective nuclear charge increases and the electron cloud contracts.
Why: A smaller, more highly polarising Ln³⁺ ion holds the OH⁻ more strongly and the bond gains covalent character, so the hydroxide releases OH⁻ less easily. Hence basicity decreases from La(OH)₃ to Lu(OH)₃. A related result: the second- and third-row transition metals of the same group (such as Zr and Hf) have almost the same radii.
Why not the others: (A) Basicity depends on ionic size and charge, not on atomic mass, and the order is reversed. (B) The charge is the same, but the size is not, so basicity differs. (D) The order is right, but the reason is wrong: 4f shielding is poor, and the ions get smaller.
Key point: La³⁺ → Lu³⁺: radius decreases → covalent character increases → basicity decreases.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Matching coordination compounds and ligands with their important uses
questions.question:
Match each substance in List I with its use in List II.

List I | List II
P EDTA (as its calcium complex) | (1) A volatile complex that decomposes on heating to give the pure metal
Q cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] | (2) Forms a red precipitate used to detect and estimate Ni²⁺
R [Ni(CO)₄] | (3) Removes lead from the body (chelation therapy)
S Dimethylglyoxime | (4) Inhibits the growth of tumours
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) P-3, Q-4, R-1, S-2.
Concept: Coordination compounds are important in analytical chemistry, metallurgy, biology and medicine. Chelating ligands form very stable complexes, which can be used to remove or detect metal ions.
Why: EDTA forms a very stable chelate with Pb²⁺, which is excreted in urine, so Ca-EDTA is used to treat lead poisoning (P-3). Cisplatin, cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], binds DNA and is used against cancer (Q-4). In the Mond process, impure nickel forms volatile [Ni(CO)₄], which is decomposed on heating to give pure nickel (R-1). Dimethylglyoxime gives a red precipitate of [Ni(dmg)₂] with Ni²⁺ (S-2).
Why not the others: (B) EDTA does not give a red precipitate with nickel, and dimethylglyoxime is not used for lead poisoning. (C) Cisplatin is not used in metal refining, and [Ni(CO)₄] is not an anticancer drug. (D) Every pair is wrong.
Key point: EDTA – lead poisoning; cisplatin – cancer; Ni(CO)₄ – Mond process; dmg – Ni²⁺ test.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Oxidation state, coordination number and number of ions for a complex with a bidentate ligand
questions.question: For the complex \(\ce{K3[Fe(C2O4)3]}\), what are the oxidation state of iron, the coordination number of iron, and the number of ions formed per formula unit in aqueous solution?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) +3; 6; 4.
Concept: In Werner's theory, the primary valence of the metal (its oxidation state) is satisfied by negative ions, and the secondary valence (coordination number) is the number of donor atoms bound to the metal. A bidentate ligand such as oxalate, \(\ce{C2O4^2-}\), binds through two donor atoms.
Why: The complex ion is [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ (balanced by 3 K⁺). Oxidation state: x + 3(−2) = −3, so x = +3. Three bidentate oxalates give 3 × 2 = 6 donor atoms, so the coordination number is 6. In water it gives 3 K⁺ + 1 [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ = 4 ions.
Why not the others: (A) It counts ligands instead of donor atoms; each oxalate binds through two oxygen atoms. (C) Fe is +3, and the salt gives 4 ions, not 2. (D) Three oxalates (−6) and a −3 complex ion need Fe³⁺, not Fe²⁺.
Key point: Coordination number = number of donor atoms (oxalate counts 2), not number of ligands.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Stereochemical outcome of SN1 hydrolysis of a tertiary halide and SN2 substitution of a secondary halide
questions.question: (S)-3-Bromo-3-methylhexane is hydrolysed in aqueous acetone, and separately (R)-2-bromooctane reacts with aqueous NaOH under SN2 conditions. Which description of the products is correct?
options: A) Both products keep the configuration of the starting halides
B) Both products are completely racemic
C) The first product has an inverted configuration, and the second is racemic

D) The first gives a nearly racemic alcohol because water attacks a planar carbocation from either face; the second gives (S)-octan-2-ol because hydroxide attacks from the side opposite to the leaving bromide
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The first gives a nearly racemic alcohol because water attacks a planar carbocation from either face; the second gives (S)-octan-2-ol because hydroxide attacks from the side opposite to the leaving bromide.
Concept: In SN1, the slow step forms a planar sp² carbocation; the nucleophile can attack either face, so an optically active substrate gives a racemic (or nearly racemic) product. In SN2, the nucleophile attacks from the back as the leaving group departs, giving inversion of configuration (Walden inversion).
Why: The tertiary bromide ionises easily in a polar solvent, so it reacts by SN1, and optical activity is largely lost. The secondary bromide with a strong nucleophile reacts by SN2; inversion turns R into S here because OH replaces Br with the same priority order.
Why not the others: (A) Neither mechanism retains configuration in this way. (B) SN2 gives a single inverted product, not a racemate. (C) The mechanisms are swapped.
Key point: SN1 → racemisation (planar carbocation); SN2 → inversion (backside attack).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Linked: products of cleavage of two different ethers by one equivalent of HI
questions.question: Methyl tert-butyl ether, \(\ce{CH3-O-C(CH3)3}\), and ethyl methyl ether, \(\ce{CH3-O-CH2CH3}\), are each treated with one equivalent of concentrated HI. What are the main products in each case?
options: A) Methyl iodide and tert-butyl alcohol; ethyl iodide and methanol
B) tert-Butyl iodide and methanol; methyl iodide and ethanol
C) tert-Butyl iodide and methanol; ethyl iodide and methanol
D) Methyl iodide and tert-butyl alcohol; methyl iodide and ethanol
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) tert-Butyl iodide and methanol; methyl iodide and ethanol.
Concept: HI first protonates the ether oxygen. Then the C–O bond breaks either by SN2 attack of I⁻ at the less hindered carbon, or, when one group is tertiary, by SN1, forming a stable tertiary carbocation that combines with I⁻.
Why: With a tert-butyl group, the protonated ether loses methanol to give (CH₃)₃C⁺, which takes up I⁻: (CH₃)₃CI + CH₃OH. With methyl and ethyl groups, I⁻ attacks the less hindered methyl carbon by SN2: CH₃I + CH₃CH₂OH.
Why not the others: (A) For the tert-butyl ether the SN1 path puts iodide on the tertiary carbon; for ethyl methyl ether iodide attacks the methyl group, not the ethyl. (C) The second case is wrong: methyl is less hindered than ethyl. (D) The first case is wrong: the tertiary carbocation route gives tert-butyl iodide.
Key point: Ether + HI: SN2 → iodide on the smaller group; tertiary group → SN1, iodide on the tertiary carbon.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reaction of a carboxylate salt that gives an alkane with one carbon fewer
questions.question: Which reaction converts a carboxylic acid (as its sodium salt) into an alkane containing one carbon atom fewer than the acid?
options: A) Kolbe electrolysis of an aqueous solution of the sodium salt
B) Heating the acid with chlorine in the presence of red phosphorus
C) Heating the sodium salt with soda lime (NaOH + CaO), for example sodium propanoate giving ethane
D) Reduction of the acid with lithium aluminium hydride
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Heating the sodium salt with soda lime (NaOH + CaO), for example sodium propanoate giving ethane.
Concept: Decarboxylation removes the –COOH group as CO₂ (here as Na₂CO₃). Sodium salts of carboxylic acids lose CO₂ when heated with soda lime: \(\ce{RCOONa + NaOH ->[CaO][\Delta] R-H + Na2CO3}\).
Why: The carboxyl carbon leaves as carbonate, so the alkane has one carbon fewer: \(\ce{CH3CH2COONa + NaOH -> CH3CH3 + Na2CO3}\).
Why not the others: (A) Kolbe electrolysis joins two alkyl groups: sodium propanoate gives butane, which has more carbon atoms than the acid. (B) This is the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction, giving an α-chloro acid, not an alkane. (D) LiAlH₄ reduces the acid to a primary alcohol with the same number of carbons.
Key point: RCOONa + soda lime → R–H (one carbon fewer); Kolbe electrolysis → R–R.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Identifying primary aliphatic, secondary and primary aromatic amines from their reactions with nitrous acid
questions.question:
Three amines X, Y and Z are ethanamine, N-methylethanamine and aniline, in some order. Each is treated with NaNO₂ and dilute HCl at 0–5 °C.

Amine | Observation
X | Bubbles of a colourless gas form at once
Y | A yellow oily layer separates
Z | A clear solution forms, which gives an orange-red dye when added to an alkaline solution of 2-naphthol

Which identification is correct?
options: A) X ethanamine, Y N-methylethanamine, Z aniline
B) X aniline, Y ethanamine, Z N-methylethanamine
C) X N-methylethanamine, Y aniline, Z ethanamine
D) X ethanamine, Y aniline, Z N-methylethanamine
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) X ethanamine, Y N-methylethanamine, Z aniline.
Concept: Nitrous acid (from NaNO₂ + HCl) distinguishes amines. Primary aliphatic amines form unstable diazonium salts that decompose at once, giving N₂ gas (and mainly alcohols). Primary aromatic amines form diazonium salts that are stable at 0–5 °C and couple with phenols to give azo dyes. Secondary amines give yellow, oily N-nitrosamines.
Why: X releases N₂ immediately → primary aliphatic (ethanamine). Y gives an oily N-nitroso compound → secondary amine (N-methylethanamine). Z gives benzenediazonium chloride, which couples with 2-naphthol to an orange-red azo dye → aniline.
Why not the others: (B) Aniline gives a stable diazonium salt at 0–5 °C, not immediate gas. (C) A secondary amine does not release N₂ or form a diazonium salt. (D) Aniline does not give an oily nitrosamine, and a secondary amine cannot form an azo dye this way.
Key point: HNO₂: 1° aliphatic → N₂; 1° aromatic → diazonium → azo dye; 2° → yellow oily N-nitrosamine.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting integer values of a coefficient for which a quadratic has integer roots
questions.question: For how many integer values of k does the equation \(x^2-kx+12=0\) have both roots integers?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 6.
Given: \(x^2-kx+12=0\ \text{with integer roots }\alpha,\beta\)
Formula/Principle: \(\alpha\beta=12,\quad \alpha+\beta=k\)
Step 1: \(\text{positive factor pairs: }(1,12),(2,6),(3,4)\Rightarrow k=13,8,7\)
Step 2: \(\text{negative pairs: }(-1,-12),(-2,-6),(-3,-4)\Rightarrow k=-13,-8,-7\)
Worked derivation: \[k\in\{\pm7,\pm8,\pm13\}\Rightarrow6\ \text{values}\]
Check: \[k=7:\ x^2-7x+12=(x-3)(x-4)\ \checkmark;\quad k=-8:\ x^2+8x+12=(x+2)(x+6)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{integer roots must be a factor pair of the constant term}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{only positive pairs}\); (B) \(\text{miscounts the pairs}\); (C) \(\text{counts ordered pairs, but }(\alpha,\beta)\ \text{and }(\beta,\alpha)\ \text{give the same }k\).
Key point: \(\text{integer roots}\Rightarrow\text{factor pairs of }c;\ \text{each unordered pair gives one }k\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Number of triangles formed from points with some collinear
questions.question: There are 12 points in a plane, of which exactly 5 lie on one straight line; no other three of the points are collinear. How many triangles can be formed with vertices at these points?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 210.
Given: \(12\ \text{points};\ 5\ \text{collinear};\ \text{no other three collinear}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{triangles}=\binom{12}{3}-\binom53\ \text{(collinear triples give no triangle)}\)
Step 1: \(\binom{12}3=220\)
Step 2: \(\binom53=10\)
Worked derivation: \[220-10=210\]
Check: \[\text{direct: }\binom73+\binom72\binom51+\binom71\binom52=35+105+70=210\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{three points on one line form a degenerate triangle with zero area}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{does not remove collinear triples}\); (C) \(\text{this is the number of distinct lines}\); (D) \(\text{removes }\binom52=10\ \text{twice}\).
Key point: \(\text{subtract the selections that fail (collinear triples)}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Sums of areas and perimeters of nested squares formed by joining midpoints (infinite G.P.)
questions.question: A square has side a. A second square is formed by joining the midpoints of its sides, a third by joining the midpoints of the sides of the second, and so on without end. What are the sum of the areas and the sum of the perimeters of all the squares?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(2a^2\); \(4(2+\sqrt2)\,a\).
Given: \(\text{first side }a;\ \text{each new side}=\tfrac12\times\text{diagonal of the previous square}\)
Formula/Principle: \(S_\infty=\dfrac{a_1}{1-r},\ |r|<1\)
Step 1: \(\text{sides: }a,\ \dfrac a{\sqrt2},\ \dfrac a2,\ldots\Rightarrow r=\dfrac1{\sqrt2}\)
Step 2: \(\text{areas: }a^2,\ \dfrac{a^2}2,\ldots;\ S=\dfrac{a^2}{1-\frac12}=2a^2\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{perimeters: }S=\frac{4a}{1-\frac1{\sqrt2}}=\frac{4\sqrt2\,a}{\sqrt2-1}=4\sqrt2(\sqrt2+1)a=4(2+\sqrt2)a\]
Check: \[\text{each new square has half the area of the previous one, and the total area }2a^2\ \text{is finite}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{lengths shrink by }1/\sqrt2\ \text{and areas by }1/2\ \text{at each step}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses ratio }\tfrac12\ \text{for perimeters}\); (B) \(\text{gives only the second terms}\); (D) \(\text{uses ratio }\tfrac14\ \text{for areas}\).
Key point: \(\text{nested midpoint squares: length ratio }1/\sqrt2,\ \text{area ratio }1/2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Locus of points at a fixed distance from a given line
questions.question: Which lines form the locus of points at a distance of 2 units from the line \(3x+4y-8=0\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(3x+4y-18=0\) and \(3x+4y+2=0\).
Given: \(\text{line }3x+4y-8=0;\ \text{distance }2\)
Formula/Principle: \(d=\dfrac{|ax_0+by_0+c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{|3x+4y-8|}{5}=2\Rightarrow|3x+4y-8|=10\)
Step 2: \(3x+4y-8=10\ \text{or}\ 3x+4y-8=-10\)
Worked derivation: \[3x+4y-18=0\quad\text{or}\quad3x+4y+2=0\]
Check: \[\text{distance between the two lines}=\frac{|-18-2|}{5}=4=2\times2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the locus is a pair of parallel lines, one on each side}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{forgets to multiply by }\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=5\); (C) \(\text{these are perpendicular to the given line}\); (D) \(\text{misses the line on the other side}\).
Key point: \(\text{lines parallel to }ax+by+c=0\ \text{at distance }d:\ ax+by+c\pm d\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=0\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Centre and radius of the circle through three given points
questions.question: What are the centre and radius of the circle passing through \((0,0)\), \((4,0)\) and \((0,6)\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Centre \((2,3)\), radius \(\sqrt{13}\).
Given: \(\text{points }(0,0),(4,0),(0,6)\)
Formula/Principle: \(x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0;\ \text{centre }(-g,-f),\ r=\sqrt{g^2+f^2-c}\)
Step 1: \((0,0):\ c=0\)
Step 2: \((4,0):\ 16+8g=0\Rightarrow g=-2;\quad (0,6):\ 36+12f=0\Rightarrow f=-3\)
Worked derivation: \[x^2+y^2-4x-6y=0:\ \text{centre }(2,3),\ r=\sqrt{4+9}=\sqrt{13}\]
Check: \[\text{the angle at }(0,0)\ \text{is }90^\circ,\ \text{so }(4,0)\text{–}(0,6)\ \text{is a diameter: midpoint }(2,3),\ \text{half-length }\tfrac12\sqrt{52}=\sqrt{13}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the angle in a semicircle is a right angle}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(13\ \text{is }r^2\); (C) \(\text{sign of the centre}\); (D) \(\text{uses the whole diameter}\).
Key point: \(\text{right angle at a vertex}\Rightarrow\text{the opposite side is a diameter}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Points of a parabola at a given focal distance
questions.question: For the parabola \(y^2=12x\), which points are at a distance of 15 units from the focus?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \((12,\pm12)\).
Given: \(y^2=12x=4ax\Rightarrow a=3;\ \text{focal distance}=15\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{focus }(a,0),\ \text{directrix }x=-a;\ \text{focal distance}=x+a\)
Step 1: \(x+3=15\Rightarrow x=12\)
Step 2: \(y^2=12\times12=144\Rightarrow y=\pm12\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{distance from }(3,0)\ \text{to }(12,12)=\sqrt{81+144}=\sqrt{225}=15\]
Check: \[\text{distance from }(12,12)\ \text{to directrix }x=-3\ \text{is }15\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{every point of a parabola is equidistant from focus and directrix}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{takes }x=15\ \text{(forgets }a)\); (B) \(y^2=36\ne144\); (C) \(x+3=12\ne15\).
Key point: \(\text{on }y^2=4ax:\ SP=x+a\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Rates of change of the area and circumference of a growing circle
questions.question: The radius of a circular ripple increases at 2 cm s⁻¹. At the instant when the radius is 5 cm, how fast are its area and its circumference increasing?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(20\pi\ \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}}\); \(4\pi\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\).
Given: \(\dfrac{dr}{dt}=2\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}},\ r=5\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(A=\pi r^2,\ C=2\pi r;\ \dfrac{dA}{dt}=\dfrac{dA}{dr}\dfrac{dr}{dt}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{dA}{dt}=2\pi r\dfrac{dr}{dt}=2\pi(5)(2)=20\pi\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dC}{dt}=2\pi\dfrac{dr}{dt}=4\pi\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{dA}{dt}=20\pi\ \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}},\qquad \frac{dC}{dt}=4\pi\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\]
Check: \[\frac{dA}{dt}=C\cdot\frac{dr}{dt}=10\pi\times2=20\pi\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the area grows by a thin ring of length }C\ \text{and width }dr\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }\pi r\ \text{instead of }2\pi r\); (C) \(\text{forgets the factor }dr/dt\ \text{in }dC/dt\); (D) \(\text{gives the area itself}\).
Key point: \(\text{chain rule: }\dfrac{dA}{dt}=A'(r)\dfrac{dr}{dt}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the contents of a bag from a given posterior probability (Bayes' theorem)
questions.question: Bag A has 3 red balls and 1 white ball. Bag B has 4 balls, of which n are red and the rest white. A bag is chosen at random and a ball drawn from it is red. If the probability that it came from bag A is \(\dfrac35\), what is n?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2.
Given: \(P(A)=P(B)=\tfrac12;\ P(R\mid A)=\tfrac34;\ P(R\mid B)=\tfrac n4;\ P(A\mid R)=\tfrac35\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(A\mid R)=\dfrac{P(A)P(R\mid A)}{P(A)P(R\mid A)+P(B)P(R\mid B)}\)
Step 1: \(P(A\mid R)=\dfrac{\frac12\cdot\frac34}{\frac12\cdot\frac34+\frac12\cdot\frac n4}=\dfrac{3}{3+n}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac3{3+n}=\dfrac35\Rightarrow3+n=5\)
Worked derivation: \[n=2\]
Check: \[P(A\mid R)=\frac{3/8}{3/8+2/8}=\frac35\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{with equal priors, the posterior ratio equals the ratio of likelihoods }3:n\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{gives }3/4\); (B) \(\text{gives }1/2\); (D) \(\text{gives }3/7\).
Key point: \(\text{equal priors}\Rightarrow P(A\mid R)=\dfrac{P(R\mid A)}{P(R\mid A)+P(R\mid B)}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Number of solutions of an equation with inverse tangents, using principal values
questions.question: How many real solutions does \(\tan^{-1}(2x)+\tan^{-1}(3x)=\dfrac\pi4\) have?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1.
Given: \(\tan^{-1}(2x)+\tan^{-1}(3x)=\tfrac\pi4\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tan(\alpha+\beta)=\dfrac{\tan\alpha+\tan\beta}{1-\tan\alpha\tan\beta};\ \tan^{-1}\in\left(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2\right)\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{2x+3x}{1-6x^2}=1\Rightarrow6x^2+5x-1=0\)
Step 2: \((6x-1)(x+1)=0\Rightarrow x=\tfrac16\ \text{or}\ x=-1\)
Step 3: \(x=-1:\ \tan^{-1}(-2)+\tan^{-1}(-3)<0\ne\tfrac\pi4\ \text{(it equals }-\tfrac{3\pi}4)\)
Worked derivation: \[x=\tfrac16:\ \tan^{-1}\tfrac13+\tan^{-1}\tfrac12=\tan^{-1}\frac{\frac13+\frac12}{1-\frac16}=\tan^{-1}1=\frac\pi4\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{LHS is increasing in }x,\ \text{so it takes the value }\pi/4\ \text{exactly once}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{taking tan of both sides can add a root whose angle sum differs by }\pi\)
Why not the others: (A) \(x=\tfrac16\ \text{works}\); (B) \(\text{keeps the extraneous root }-1\); (C) \(\text{a quadratic has at most two roots}\).
Key point: \(\text{after taking tan, check each root in the original equation}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Conditions on two parameters for a 3 × 3 linear system to have a unique, no or infinitely many solutions
questions.question: For the system \(x+y+z=6\), \(x+2y+3z=10\), \(x+2y+\lambda z=\mu\), which statement is correct?
options: A) Unique solution if \(\lambda\ne3\); no solution if \(\lambda=3,\ \mu=10\)
B) Unique solution if and only if \(\mu\ne10\)
C) Unique solution if \(\lambda\ne3\); infinitely many if \(\lambda=3,\ \mu=10\); no solution if \(\lambda=3,\ \mu\ne10\)
questions.explanation:
